facts.text: Policies prescribe. They do not propose, persuade, or describe - they bind. A reader of a policy needs three things in the first 60 seconds: who is bound by it, what they must do, and what happens if they don't.
RFC 8174 clarification: The normative meaning attaches only when the keyword is in ALL CAPITALS. Lowercase "must", "should", and "may" carry their normal English meaning and have no normative weight.

Required incantation: > The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

facets.title: 2. The policy / standard / procedure / guideline hierarchy (NIST SP 800-12)

facts.text: Policy - what must be true, and why. Mandatory. Strategic. Changes rarely.
Standard - which specific implementation satisfies the policy (TLS 1.3, AES-256). Mandatory. Tactical.
Procedure - how to perform a specific task. Mandatory for the role performing the task. Operational.
Guideline - suggested approach when no mandatory standard applies. Advisory.
The hierarchy test: if you can answer "yes" to "would this need to change when we upgrade the firewall?", it is not a policy. It is a standard or procedure.

facets.title: 3. Required components of an enforceable policy

facts.text: Title and identifier - unique policy ID, version number, effective date
Purpose - one-paragraph statement of why the policy exists
Scope - who, what, where the policy applies; explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists
Definitions - every term of art, listed alphabetically
Policy statements - the normative rules, using BCP 14 keywords in ALL CAPS
Roles and responsibilities - named role titles (not individuals) mapped to obligations
Exceptions - how to request and approve a documented deviation
Enforcement - consequences of violation
Related documents - pointers to standards, procedures, and laws
Review schedule - review cadence, owner, next review date, change-history table

facets.title: 4. The scope section as the contract boundary

facts.text: A defensible scope section answers:
People - which employees, contractors, vendors, partners, customers?
Assets - which systems, data classifications, networks, locations, devices?
Activities - which operations, transactions, or behaviors?
State each as an inclusion list AND an exclusion list.
A well-built exception clause has four elements:
Who can grant - the approval authority (named role, not person)
What must be documented - business justification, compensating controls, scope, duration
How long it lasts - maximum duration before re-review (typically 90 or 180 days)
How it is tracked - where the exception register lives
ISO/IEC 27001 clause 7.5.3 requires that documents be reviewed and updated as necessary.
Review cadence - at least annual
Document owner - the role accountable for triggering review
Change-history table - a row per version showing version, date, author, change summary, approver
The descriptive policy - lots of background, no rules.
Lowercase normatives - using "should" and "must" in lowercase while believing they bind readers.
The grab-bag scope - "This policy applies to everyone and everything." Unenforceable.
Personal-name responsibilities - "Jane Smith MUST approve all exceptions." Jane leaves; policy breaks.
No exception path - forces operators to violate or route around.
Procedure leakage - step-by-step instructions inside a policy.
The standard masquerading as policy - "All servers MUST run TLS 1.3." When TLS 1.4 ships, the policy is wrong.
